source.title: Sometimes less is more: Investigating inductive biases of MLPs and Transformers on noisy k-parity features

record.file_problem: Full paper text, including appendices, is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study measures training and held-out accuracy and how data size and training budget affect them, but only on synthetic noisy k-parity tasks. It extends generalization evidence to a new setting; it does not test the listed natural-data versions.
record.gate_note: The paper does not compare fitting random labels with fitting natural labels. Its k-parity experiments report train and test accuracy on noiseless synthetic labels, including cases where the models fit and generalize and cases where they overfit or remain undertrained. These results bear on train-test generalization in a synthetic setting, but not on the versions' specified natural-data experiments.
record.test_reason: The study reports synthetic k-parity learning and optimization results, but none tests V1–V8. Measuring train and test accuracy alone does not test V1's random-label versus natural-label comparison. Width sweeps use fixed training budgets without establishing behavior beyond an interpolation threshold; the other versions' required comparisons are absent.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors conclude that Transformers are relatively robust to noisy k-parity features but struggle with complex, low-availability features. Greater data diversity slows their optimization under fixed budgets; scaling the budget extends the learnable-feature frontier but leaves some slowdown. These conclusions concern the tested synthetic tasks and architecture-plus-training configurations, whose parameter counts, regularization, and learning rates differ.
record.recipe_differences: Synthetic k-parity experiments; compares a three-layer MLP with a three-block decoder-only Transformer. Uses Adam for the MLP and AdamW for GPT, distinct learning rates and regularization, and does not match parameter count, FLOPs, or another single scale axis.
record.method_sensitivity: Data-set size and data diversity, feature size and predictivity, model width, training-iteration budget, and whether the training set is finite or sampled directly from the DGP affect reported outcomes. Batch size is held at 256; the authors state batch-size effects are future work.

fits_no_version.finding: At d = 18, fixed-budget GPT accuracy changes from train/test 0.993/0.537 at N = 2,400 to 0.889/0.757 at N = 8,000 and 0.506/0.501 at N = 80,000. Scaled budgets reach 1.000/1.000 at N = 80,000 and 240,000. At d = 22, training accuracy falls from 0.904 at N = 24,000 to 0.771 at N = 240,000 despite ten times the iteration budget.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: On synthetic k-parity, dataset size and training budget govern overfitting and optimization speed: smaller datasets can perform better within fixed iteration budgets, while scaled budgets extend the learnable-feature frontier without eliminating every optimization slowdown.

record.problems: The experiments use synthetic uniformly sampled k-parity data, not natural data. The MLP and GPT differ in parameter count, input format, regularization, and learning rate, limiting architecture comparisons. Some regimes do not fit training data within the allotted budget, so their outcomes reflect optimization speed rather than ultimate capacity. Results are averaged across at least 5 seeds; standard deviations are shown where relevant, but Table 1 provides no uncertainty values.
record.rows_left_out: No additional rows extracted from figure-only sweeps or the noisy, two-feature, and multi-feature experiments. Their reported results concern synthetic feature learning and do not test any listed version; the selected Table 1 rows provide the explicit train/test results most directly relevant to the generalization-gap subject.

untested.parts: No comparison of fixed random-label fitting against natural-label generalization using the same architecture and recipe.
No converged width sweep establishing whether test error keeps falling beyond the width required for zero training error. Appendix D instead studies width under fixed iteration budgets.
No convolutional versus fully connected image-classification comparison or local-connectivity experiment.
No adaptive-optimizer versus SGD comparison, tuning comparison, switching experiment, or weight-decay ablation.
Batch size remains 256; no comparison of batch sizes under fixed epoch budgets.
No controlled dropout or joint dropout/weight-decay removal experiment.
No magnitude-aware sharpness measurements or comparison of generalization-gap rankings.
No identification and removal of memorized examples followed by retraining against random-removal controls.

record.verdict_notes: All extracted accuracy values agree with Table 1. States are cannot_determine relative to V1–V8 because every row links to none; this does not invalidate the synthetic results. The record's tests/T3 classification incorrectly treats general relevance to generalization as testing a specified claim version.

versions.untested_parts: No random-label experiment or natural-label benchmark; no small Inception, AlexNet, CIFAR-10, or ImageNet random-label comparison.
The study varies model width, but does not test one-hidden-layer ReLU networks on MNIST or downsampled CIFAR-10, or report a width sweep showing test error beyond the zero-training-error threshold.
MLP and Transformer results concern synthetic k-parity, not convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers or local connectivity.
The study uses Adam for MLPs and AdamW for Transformers, but does not compare adaptive optimizers against SGD or test optimizer tuning, switching, or decoupled weight decay effects.
The study varies training-set size and iteration budget, not batch size; batch size is fixed at 256. It does not compare large and small batches under fixed epoch budgets.
The study does not ablate dropout or weight decay. Its MLP uses neither; its GPT uses dropout and weight decay, but these are not varied.
No sharpness, weight-perturbation tolerance, norm, or margin measures are evaluated.
The study does not identify or remove memorized examples and retrain.
